newsitem.title: USA: CoreStates, Signet report higher profits.
newsitem.headline: CoreStates, Signet report higher profits.

text.p: CoreStates Financial Corp. and Signet Banking Corp. reported higher fourth-quarter profits Wednesday, making them the latest banks to post strong year-end results.

But Detroit-based Comerica Inc. said it would eliminate about 1,890 jobs, or about 16 percent of its work force, as part of a comprehensive effort to cut expenses and boost revenues, and said the move would hurt the bank holding company's fourth-quarter earnings.
On Tuesday, Chase Manhattan Corp. and Citicorp posted healthy profit gains, continuing a trend among large banks.
Philadelphia-based CoreStates reported net income of $195.5 million, or 91 cents a share, for the quarter, compared with net income of $192.2 million, or 87 cents per share, in 1995's fourth quarter.
CoreStates attributed the improvement in earnings to moderate growth in loans and significant reductions in non-financial expenses.
"Overall, we continued the strong operating performance that CoreStates has delivered consistently during the 1990s," Chairman Terrance Larsen said in a statement.
CoreStates stock rose $1.125 on $52.625 in late trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
Signet posted net income for the quarter of $33.6 million, or 55 cents a share, compared with $9 million, or 15 cents a share, a year ago.

The Richmond, Va.-based bank's 1995 results included charges for a commercial fraud loss and earnings of Capital One Financial Corp. before its spin-off to shareholders in February 1995. Adjusting for those items, Signet's net income rose 6 percent over the year-ago period.
The company said the increase in earnings was due to "robust growth" in consumer and commercial loans.
Signet stock rose 25 cents to $30.50 on the NYSE.

Comerica said the job cuts and other restructuring actions caused it to incur a $90 million pretax charge, or 54 cents per share, against fourth-quarter earnings, which dropped to $60.8 million, or 52 cents a year, from $106.5 million, or 92 cents a share, a year ago.

Comerica said the number of employees to be laid off may be less than 1,890 due to normal attrition, a hiring freeze and other actions. The layoffs and other streamlining were expected to boost revenues by $110 million annually by the first half of 1998.
Comerica stock slipped 37.5 cents to $55.875 on the NYSE.
